Abstract.AbstractText: Sleep is a naturally recurring physiologic state that follows the daily circadian rhythm and is characterized by reduced responsiveness to external stimuli, diminished voluntary motor activity, and reversible disengagement from the surrounding environment. Unlike coma or pathologic unconsciousness, sleep is readily reversible and is associated with predictable neurophysiologic patterns that recur cyclically throughout the night. Sleep also fundamentally differs from anesthesia and hibernation in regulatory mechanisms and the maintenance of organized endogenous neural activity. Anesthesia involves pharmacologically induced suppression of consciousness, whereas hibernation reflects a prolonged adaptive hypometabolic state. Physiologic sleep, by contrast, is an actively regulated biologic process essential for survival and systemic homeostasis. Sleep was historically believed to be a passive state. However, contemporary neurophysiologic research has established sleep as a highly dynamic and metabolically active process governed by complex interactions among cortical, hypothalamic, thalamic, and brainstem networks. [Source: Pelayo and Dement. History of Sleep Physiology and Medicine. 2016] Sleep architecture is tightly organized into alternating cycles of nonrapid (NREM) and rapid (REM) eye movement sleep, with each stage associated with distinct electrophysiologic, neurochemical, autonomic, and behavioral characteristics. These recurrent oscillations are coordinated through interactions between circadian timing systems and homeostatic mechanisms regulating sleep. [Source: Carskadon and Dement. Normal Human Sleep: An Overview. 2016] Sleep is indispensable for maintaining normal physiologic function across multiple organ systems. Experimental sleep deprivation studies have demonstrated adverse effects on cognition, metabolic regulation, immune activity, cardiovascular stability, and emotional processing. Chronic sleep disruption has additionally been associated with increased risks of obesity, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, neurodegenerative disease, mood disorders, and impaired host defense mechanisms. [Source: Banks et al. Sleep Deprivation. 2016] Increasing evidence further supports a role for sleep in glymphatic clearance of neurotoxic metabolites from the central nervous system (CNS), including β-amyloid peptides implicated in neurodegenerative disorders. Overall, understanding sleep physiology carries broad clinical relevance. Dysregulation of sleep architecture and sleep-wake control mechanisms contributes to numerous disorders, including insomnia, narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), circadian rhythm disorders, parasomnias, depression, and neurodegenerative disease. Sleep physiology also holds increasing importance in critical care medicine, perioperative management, psychiatry, neurology, and cardiovascular medicine, where disturbances in normal sleep patterns may significantly influence treatment regimens and clinical outcomes. This activity reviews the physiologic organization of sleep, including sleep architecture, neuroanatomic regulation, neurochemical mechanisms, circadian control systems, and the functional significance of REM and NREM sleep in maintaining systemic and neurologic homeostasis. Overview of Sleep Architecture Sleep is a structured sequence of distinct neurophysiologic states. Examination of sleep's architecture provides a basis for understanding its temporal and neurophysiologic characteristics. Sleep stages Human sleep is broadly divided into 2 types: NREM (slow-wave sleep; SWS) and REM. NREM sleep is characterized by progressive reductions in cortical activation, autonomic activity, and responsiveness to external stimuli. NREM sleep constitutes approximately 75% to 80% of total sleep time in healthy adults, whereas REM sleep accounts for the remaining 20% to 25%. NREM sleep is further subdivided into stages N1, N2, and N3 according to standardized polysomnographic criteria established by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM). [Source: AASM. The AASM Manual for the Scoring of Sleep and Associated Events: Rules, Terminology and Technical Specifications version 2.4. 2017] Transition through NREM stages is accompanied by increasing electroencephalographic (EEG) synchronization and progressive slowing of cortical activity. REM sleep, by contrast, is characterized by an activated EEG pattern and is generally not subdivided into stages, although some research classifications recognize additional distinctions. Electroencephalographic correlates of sleep stages EEG serves as a central tool for characterizing sleep architecture and differentiating sleep stages. Wakefulness with relaxed, closed eyes is typically associated with α waves ranging from 8 to 13 Hz, whereas alert wakefulness demonstrates higher-frequency β activity. EEG activity during NREM sleep demonstrates θ activity in stage N1, sleep spindles and K-complexes in stage N2, and dominant δ activity in stage N3. In contrast, REM sleep demonstrates low-voltage, mixed-frequency EEG activity resembling wakefulness despite concurrent muscle atonia. Sleep cycles Normal adult sleep is organized into cyclic ultradian rhythms that alternate between NREM and REM sleep approximately every 90 to 110 minutes. [Source: Tian, et al. A hierarchical classification method for automatic sleep scoring using multiscale entropy features and proportion information of sleep architecture. 2017] A typical night consists of 4 to 6 such cycles, with each cycle progressing through deeper NREM stages followed by REM sleep. NREM sleep predominates during the 1st half of the sleep period, when homeostatic sleep pressure is greatest. In contrast, REM sleep episodes become progressively longer and more frequent during the 2nd half of the night. Early REM periods may last only several minutes, whereas later episodes can exceed 30 minutes in duration. Time spent in these sleep stages has important neurophysiological implications for learning, memory, and synaptogenesis, particularly during childhood and adolescence, when brain development is ongoing. Sleep continuity and architecture are influenced by interactions between the circadian timing system and homeostatic sleep drive, as discussed in subsequent sections. Circadian signals originating from the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) regulate REM propensity and sleep-wake transitions, whereas homeostatic mechanisms increase the pressure for SWS following prolonged wakefulness.

Article.ArticleTitle: Impact of REM sleep deprivation during the acquisition phase on learning and memory performance, neurotrophic and oxidative stress markers in male rats.

Abstract.AbstractText: During adolescence, the brain is particularly vulnerable to sleep disruption, which may lead to long‑term memory deficits and emotional dysregulation. This study investigated the impact of REM sleep deprivation (REM‑SD), applied specifically during the acquisition phase of learning, on spatial memory, anxiety‑like behavior, and hippocampal neurotrophic and oxidative status in adolescent rats. Male adolescent Wistar Albino rats were subjected to a REM‑SD protocol using the modified multiple platform method (MMPM), integrated directly into the training phase of the Morris water maze (MWM). Animals were divided into three groups: Control, Pedestal Control, and REM‑SD. Anxiety‑like behavior was assessed using the open field (OFT) and elevated plus maze (EPM) tests. Corticosterone levels and hippocampal levels of nerve growth factor (NGF), brain‑derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), total oxidant status (TOS), total antioxidant status (TAS), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and malondialdehyde (MDA) were analyzed by ELISA. REM‑SD during the acquisition phase significantly impaired memory performance in the MWM probe trial. In the OFT test, REM‑SD rats exhibited increased anxiety‑like behavior, reflected by reduced time spent in the center zone, whereas the EPM demonstrated increased open‑arm duration. These behavioral alterations were accompanied by significantly elevated corticosterone levels. REM‑SD was associated with reduced hippocampal antioxidant status (decreased TAS and SOD), decreased NGF levels, and increased oxidative status (TOS). Our findings demonstrate that exposure to the MMPM, together with REM sleep disruption and associated stress‑related physiological responses, was accompanied by alterations in memory performance, corticosterone levels, oxidative balance, and neurotrophic markers. The observed behavioral changes, including alterations during late acquisition and impaired probe trial performance, may reflect combined effects on learning‑ and memory‑related processes.
